original_question: Let d_n = (p_{n+1} - p_n)/2, where p_n is the nth prime. Determine whether the sequence (d_n) contains infinitely many primes, whether it contains values of the form n!, and whether it contains values of the form n^n. More generally, for higher-order derived sequences formed from prime gaps, ask the same questions.
target_in_paper: Unsolved Problem 12, the paper's question about the halved gaps between consecutive primes, first for d_n = (p_{n+1} - p_n)/2 and then for the explicitly introduced related sequences d_n^(i) and d_{n,i}^{(i-1)}. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the base sequence d_n = (p_{n+1} - p_n)/2, the three specific pattern-questions in the paper (prime values, values of the form n!, and values of the form n^n), and the fact that the paper then extends the same questions to additional sequences built from prime gaps. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
missing_details: The official target is exactly Unsolved Problem 12; the draft should be tied to that narrower formulation rather than to a broader prime-gap research program. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
The paper uses p_n for the n-th prime, indexes n = 1, 2, ..., and in the extension uses i in N*, where N* denotes the positive integers. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

Only the prime-values question is asked with infinitude ('Does d_n contain an infinite number of primes?'); the questions about n! and n^n are occurrence questions, not infinitude questions. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

The generalization is not stated vaguely as 'higher-order derived sequences'; the paper explicitly introduces, for each i in N*, the sequence d_n^(i) = (p_{n+i} - p_n)/2 and also the sequence written there as d_{n,i}^{(i-1)} = (d_{n+1} - d_n)/2, followed by 'The same questions.' ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
A stand-alone formulation should avoid overloading the symbol n in both the sequence index and the forms n!, n^n; using a second variable such as m makes the question precise.

Under the standard indexing p_1 = 2, the first term is d_1 = 1/2, so the sequence is not entirely integral; a self-contained rewrite should make clear that the question is whether some terms equal prime integers, factorials, or m^m values. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
refined_question: Let p_n be the n-th prime (with p_1 = 2), and for n = 1, 2, ... define d_n = (p_{n+1} - p_n)/2. Does the set of values of the sequence (d_n) contain infinitely many prime integers? Does it contain a value of the form m! for some positive integer m? Does it contain a value of the form m^m for some positive integer m? More generally, for each i in N* = {1,2,3,...}, define d_n^(i) = (p_{n+i} - p_n)/2 for n = 1, 2, ..., and also consider the related sequence written in the paper as d_{n,i}^{(i-1)} = (d_{n+1} - d_n)/2. For each of these sequences, ask the same three questions. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
justification: The draft is clearly aimed at Unsolved Problem 12, whose first sentence and three follow-up questions it reproduces in substance. The main repairs needed for paper-faithfulness are: (1) keep the quantifier asymmetry from the source text, where infinitude is asked only for prime-valued terms; (2) replace the vague final clause by the paper's actual extension to the named sequences d_n^(i) and d_{n,i}^{(i-1)}; and (3) make the indexing and notation self-contained. This paper is a list of unsolved problems rather than a theorem/proposition paper, so there is no nearby proved equivalence to report; the sharpest faithful rewrite is therefore a cleaned-up restatement of Unsolved Problem 12 itself. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
